summary: Jesús Barrasa (Neo4j AI Field CTO) argues ontologies provide a practical middle ground between rigid code-orchestrated workflows and chaotic LLM-driven behavior in agent design. The talk centers on GraphRAG, where a knowledge graph replaces the vector database in RAG, offering richer retrieval: vector semantic search plus graph contextualization, structured query generation, navigation, enrichment, filtering, and aggregation—yielding better completeness, precision, relevance, and faithfulness. The Neo4j property graph model has two primitives: nodes (entities with key-value properties) and directed relationships. Graphs built from unstructured data combine a domain graph (entities, relationships) with a lexical graph (documents, chunks, hierarchical structure for legal documents) connected via entity extraction; chunk nodes also store vector embeddings, unifying vector search and connected data in one platform. Building graphs requires passing a target schema—different pipelines (structured data mapping, LangChain/LlamaIndex integrations, LLM extraction) use divergent schema representations (JSON, Pydantic, natural language). Ontologies solve this divergence as implementation-agnostic formal schemas (W3C standards, multiple serializations including XML and JSON). Barrasa demonstrates with the FIBO financial ontology: classes with subclass relationships and cross-class connections map naturally to graph models. He strongly advocates a model-driven approach, arguing it improves both graph construction quality and downstream retrieval—better text-to-structured-query generation and better vector-plus-contextualization results. On the retrieval side, vector search over embedded chunk properties creates an entry point into the graph; once proximate vectors are found, they are dereferenced back to graph nodes, enabling contextualization through navigation, enrichment, filtering, and aggregation. A code example using a movie database shows querying embedded movie plots with top-K retrieval. Barrasa then addresses a key limitation of hardcoded retrievers: building a retrieval query requires knowing the graph model (actors acted in movies, movies have plots), making the retriever rigid. The solution is to persist the ontology in the graph alongside the data and create dynamic queries that consult the ontology at runtime. By annotating certain ontology relationships as contextualizing relationships, the retriever dynamically navigates only those relationships—for example, when retrieving The Matrix, it follows actor-in relationships but not producer or directed-by. This provides a level of indirection: changing the ontology (a data artifact in the graph) changes retriever behavior on the fly without code changes. Barrasa concludes with two takeaways: ontologies serve as implementation-agnostic data models for knowledge graph creation, and storing ontologies in the graph can drive dynamic behavior in retrievers.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and GraphRAG Overview
sections.summary: Barrasa introduces himself and the talk's focus on ontologies for GraphRAG. He explains GraphRAG as RAG with a knowledge graph replacing the vector database, enabling richer retrieval strategies (vector search, contextualization via graph connections, structured queries) that improve completeness, precision, relevance, and faithfulness.

sections.title: Property Graph Model and Graph Construction
sections.summary: Describes the Neo4j property graph model (nodes as entities with key-value properties, directed relationships), the domain graph vs. lexical graph distinction, and how chunk nodes store both text and vector embeddings. Covers building graphs from structured data (schema mapping via Neo4j UI/API) and unstructured data (document splitting, embedding, entity extraction with schema injection), noting divergent schema representations across pipelines.

sections.title: Ontologies as Implementation-Agnostic Schemas
sections.summary: Introduces ontologies as W3C-standardized, implementation-agnostic formal schemas that eliminate pipeline divergence. Uses the FIBO financial ontology to illustrate classes, subclass hierarchies, and cross-class relationships mapping to graph models. Advocates a model-driven approach for better graph construction and downstream retrieval quality.

sections.title: Retrieval Mechanism and Code Example
sections.summary: Explains how vector search over embedded chunk properties creates an entry point into the graph; proximate vectors are dereferenced to nodes for contextualization via navigation, enrichment, filtering, and aggregation. Shows a Python code example querying embedded movie plots with top-K retrieval.

sections.title: Dynamic Ontology-Driven Retrievers
sections.summary: Addresses the rigidity of hardcoded retrieval queries that require intimate knowledge of the graph model. The solution is persisting the ontology in the graph and creating dynamic queries that consult the ontology at runtime for relationships annotated as contextualizing relationships. This provides a level of indirection—changing the ontology (a data artifact) changes retriever behavior on the fly without code modifications. Barrasa concludes with two takeaways: ontologies for implementation-agnostic KG creation, and stored ontologies driving dynamic retriever behavior.

demonstrations: Neo4j UI for mapping structured data sources to a graph model, populating nodes and relationships based on a target schema

limitations: No time to walk through the combined structured/unstructured data ontology example in detail

Cypher expertise needed to fully understand the dynamic ontology-driven query approach
